paras: The South Side Chicago boys' riot of April 1919 was a fight between white and Black boys, taken up by their parents, in a South Side neighborhood of Chicago, Illinois, during the last week of April 1919, in which William Epps, a 23-year-old Black man, was shot. Police reserves ended the fighting, and Epps was reported to be at the point of death in Provident Hospital. The Associated Negro Press disputed the Chicago dailies' account of how it began, and Black weeklies across the country printed its version.

The fight took place in a South Side neighborhood that had recently seen bomb throwing, which the ANP tied to Black families occupying homes formerly held by white residents. The Baltimore Afro-American likewise placed the disturbance near the recent bombings.

According to the daily papers, as the ANP summarized them, two white boys passing on bicycles were stoned by Black boys and went to get other boys to "clean up the gang." Older persons and the boys' parents joined them with sticks, bricks, bats and guns, and the Black boys' parents and other adults answered "by the same token." The calling out of the police reserves brought what the dispatch called a quick end to what might have been a very serious event.

In the course of the fighting William Epps, 23, was shot, and he was taken to Provident Hospital, where he lay at the point of death. None of the reports says who fired the shot. The Baltimore Afro-American, in a separately worded item datelined May 1, said one man was in the hospital in serious condition and that the disturbance had begun among white and colored boys before being "taken up by the parents."

The Chicago Tribune, as quoted by the ANP, answered the clash with a lengthy editorial titled "Racial Neighborliness," which called it the result of "misdirected energy, spontaneous as to time and place" rather than evidence of racial friction. The editorial urged an immediate commission to investigate and report on the social welfare of the races. No later report of Epps's death or recovery, of arrests, or of an inquest was found in the coverage.

Black coverage rested almost entirely on a single ANP dispatch, which the Black Dispatch and the St. Louis Argus printed on May 2 and the Cleveland Advocate, the Dallas Express and the Phoenix Tribune on May 3. The dispatch set the dailies' story against its own investigations, which blamed "rowdy white boys" for interfering with a little Black girl at a confectionery.

Headlines weighted the same text differently: the Black Dispatch called it "The Old, Old Story" and declared that whites start riots when women of the race get the protection they ought to have, while the Dallas Express ran "Children's Fracas Causes Young Riot in Chicago" over a deck about Black boys protecting a little girl from "White Rowdies." The Phoenix Tribune ("Riot Narrowly Averted Through the Action of Bad Youngsters") and the Cleveland Advocate ("Near Riot in Chicago") stressed how close the affair came to something larger, while the Argus led with the bomb throwing and the Tribune's call for an investigation.

The Chicago Defender's editorial page that week did not name the incident, but its editorial "Reducing Friction" complained that daily papers turned schoolchildren's fights "with sticks, stones and probably fists" into race riots in order to intensify race hatred. At the end of May an ANP item in the Omaha Monitor and the Dallas Express quoted a Georgia paper that cited "a serious riot" between whites and Blacks in Chicago "the other day" as a reason Black migrants should return South, without saying which clash it meant.

The two accounts of the cause both reached readers through the ANP dispatch: the daily papers said Black boys stoned white cyclists first, while the ANP said white boys began the trouble by interfering with a Black girl, and neither version names a witness. The Black Dispatch copy, heavily damaged in print, is datelined April 29 rather than May 1 and says the riot caused Epps's "arrest" rather than his shooting, though it keeps the phrase about his lying near death in the hospital.

reader.title: South Side Chicago boys' riot of April 1919
bases: White boys joined by older persons and parents armed with sticks, bricks, bats and guns set out to 'clean up the gang' of Black boys, Black adults answered in kind, and a Black man, William Epps, was shot (A3, A11, A1); no attack on homes is reported.

The ANP dispatch (A3, A11, A2) and the separately worded Baltimore Afro-American brief (A1) agree that a fight among white and Black boys taken up by parents put one man in the hospital and was ended by police reserves near the scene of recent bombings; they differ only on how it began (A3, A11).

framing.detail: The Black Dispatch headlined the ANP story 'The Old, Old Story, Whites Start Riot When Women of the Race Get Protection That They Ought to Have.'

The ANP dispatch, run in the Argus, Phoenix Tribune, Cleveland Advocate and Dallas Express, said the dailies' account of the cause was 'at variance' with its own investigation and blamed 'rowdy white boys'.
The Phoenix Tribune's headline 'Riot Narrowly Averted Through the Action of Bad Youngsters' and the Dallas Express's 'Children's Fracas' treated it as a boys' fight that nearly became a riot.
The Chicago Defender editorial 'Reducing Friction', without naming an incident, accused daily papers of turning schoolchildren's fights into 'race riots' to intensify race hatred.
